4558.prule: Word stress on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic content words (Costello 2014); in Bradley 1970's terms the microstress falls on the tonic syllable of the microsegment, i.e. the first syllable of the bisyllabic couplet, which is always followed by exactly one posttonic syllable; pretonic syllables (prefixes) precede it (/ka'hoo/ 'box', /ma'we?e/ 'this particular house'). Monosyllables and a few bisyllabic function words are unstressed.
4558.srule: None within the word: Costello 2014 (sec. 3.2, p. 25) mentions no secondary stress, and Bradley 1970 (sec. 1.25 p. 13, 1.4 p. 17, 1.5 pp. 19-21) gives each microsegment (couplet) a single microstress with atonic pre- and postmicrosegment syllables; his second degree, macrostress, is the phrase (macrosegment) peak and 'falls on the syllable of a microsegment that in other environments bears merely the microstress' (p. 20).

4560.prule: Stress is an intensity accent riding on the HIGH level of a three-level (H/M/L), non-contrastive pitch pattern whose shape is 'casi predecible' from syllable count: disyllables H-L = stress on the first syllable (kinship terms L-H = final, 28 of 32 terms); trisyllables M-H-L = stress on the second syllable (H-H-L 'de muy baja frecuencia'); four-syllable words one of three patterns (M-H-M-L, H-H-H-L, M-H-H-L) with 'un acento primario y uno secundario, o dos acentos primarios' and no single position; five-syllable words (mostly compounds) 'siempre' two primary stresses, on the second syllable and the penult ('excepto unos pocos nombres que lo llevan en la última'). Occasionally stress falls on a final low-toned syllable. Suffixation moves the H/stress one syllable to the right (['júkɨ] 'árbol' → [jū'kɨgɨ]). quantity-insensitive: syllables are (C)V. Grids the source fixes: 2σ 10, 3σ 010, 5σ 01010 (two primaries); 4σ not fixed.
4560.srule: Exists, placement not given: four-syllable words may have 'un acento primario y uno secundario, o dos acentos primarios'; the source does not say which syllable carries the secondary. Two- and three-syllable words have a single stress; the two stresses of five-syllable words are both called primary (see primary rule).

4560.tone: Three pitch levels (alto, medio, bajo; muy alto/muy bajo by position in the intonation contour). The author finds no distinctive function at any level ('no le hemos hallado valor fonológico en ningún nivel de la lengua', p. 382), judges that 'el pisamira no sea una lengua tonal' (p. 382) and excludes tone from the phonemic transcription (p. 383), while noting that cognates differ from Bará/Tatuyo/Tucano only by tone pattern (Cuadro 3). Stress is the intensity correlate of the H level. Tone and stress 'varían de posición también en forma arbitraria' in CVV words and in vowel sequences with /a/ (p. 383). Later work reported second-hand in Rodríguez Preciado 2018 (§2.5, pp. 35-36): Valderrama 2014 finds tone patterns depend on syllable count and stress always falls on the H syllable 'pero no deja clara la función fonológica'; Gómez-Imbert 2011a p. 1451 groups Pisamira with Tuyuca/Desano/Siriano/Yurutí as having one H mora per word, i.e. a culminative pitch-accent analysis is possible; Rodríguez Preciado herself (p. 155) says she could corroborate tonal distinctions empirically but does not analyse them.

4563.tone: Phong is described as a four-tone language following the general Tangsa-Nocte tone categorisation (p. 234; Table 9.1 p. 235): T1 low falling with creak/glottalisation (not limited to open syllables), T2 mid delayed-falling modal, T3 mid level breathy (breathiness 'almost prevalent enough as to be considered a primary feature of the toneme', p. 235), T4 'short, high and checked' (p. 239). Some lexemes have shifted category relative to cognates ('head' /kʰu3/ vs T2 elsewhere; 'stamping' /nak4/ vs T1 elsewhere). Tone sandhi: complete regressive neutralisation of a T1/T2 first syllable of a bisyllabic compound to a mid-level T3-like contour ('leech' /si3 vət4/ < /si1/ 'blood'); T3 final aspiration elided non-finally. Stress: the thesis says nothing Phong-specific; at group level (sec. 5.1.3 p. 94; repeated p. 171 'sesquisyllabic causative prefix... by definition toneless and unstressed' and Fig. 7.9 caption 'sesquisyllabic prefixes... are unstressed and atonal') the presyllable is toneless and unstressed and is marked tone 0 (Phong example /i0 ma1/ 'scar', p. 235). The intonation discussion elsewhere in the thesis notes emphasis 'happens through lengthening and stress' at utterance level; that is not a word-stress rule.

4568.heavy: A syllable containing a long vowel (a sequence of two like vowels, including across a morpheme boundary) or a rising diphthong (/ai, au/ most commonly; also /ei, eu, ae, ao, oi, ou/; level sequences /eo, oe, io/ normally behave alike, /iu, ui/ variably). Falling vowel sequences /ia, ua, ie, ue, ea, oa, uo/ are not stress units. The language has no closed syllables.
4568.dflt: Penultimate mora, i.e. penultimate syllable of an all-light word, with alternating secondary stress on every second syllable leftward (source: 'This rule correctly predicts the stress placement on a word with any number of syllables of the form CV'; examples paka, pepeke, winangalo, mangamanga, Kilitimeti).
4568.prule: Mora-counting rule: stress falls on the vowel of the penultimate mora of the word and on every second mora to its left. A long vowel (two like vowels) or a rising diphthong is bimoraic and takes stress as a unit on its first vowel (stress shifted back to the syllable start if the count lands on its second mora); no two successive morae are stressed. Primary stress falls on the syllable containing a long vowel or rising diphthong (a long vowel outranks a rising diphthong; with two such syllables the first is marginally stronger); if the word has none, primary stress is on the penultimate mora (= penultimate syllable in all-light words). Falling vowel sequences /ia ua ie ue ea oa uo/ count as two separate morae, so word-final stress arises on words ending in a long vowel or rising diphthong (akalaa, manamanataa).
4568.srule: Secondary stresses are the non-primary positions of the penultimate-mora count: the penultimate mora and every second mora to its left are stressed (long vowels and rising diphthongs as units; each morpheme of a complex word counted separately), the primary being the one on a long-vowel or rising-diphthong syllable, else the penultimate mora; the others are secondary, preceding the primary in all-light or final-heavy words (lòtotónu, màtawíti, àkaláa, mànamànatáa) and falling on the penultimate mora when the primary is on an earlier heavy syllable (máalàma, uwáilèti).

sources.text: "Stress is mobile (except in Yich K'ox). This mobility allows words to be stressed in two ways: in the first, stress falls on the last syllable of a word in isolation or of a word used at the end of a phrase. In the second, stress falls on the first syllable of a word placed inside a phrase. Excepted from this stress pattern is Yich K'ox, which uses fixed stress on the last syllable of the word regardless of context."

4581.dloc: Clairis 1977 p. 152, section 'Prosodie et groupe des phonèmes'. Aguilera 1978 p. 58.
4581.heavy: Not stated. Aguilera 1978: 58 says placement is 'regulada por reglas que funcionan de acuerdo a la estructura de los núcleos vocálicos y los grupos silábicos' (which could hint at weight) but gives no rule; the announced separate publication (Aguilera 1978c ms.; presumably Aguilera 1982/1983) is not reachable.
4581.prule: No fixed position. Clairis 1977: stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable, but there are exceptions and its place cannot always be predicted; in many cases the accent can be moved without the informant taking notice, and units were often heard with no syllable (or every syllable) prominent. Aguilera 1978: stress is 'libre', falling on any of the last three syllables of uninflected (thematic) forms and shifting in suffixed (compound) forms; Aguilera's promised placement rules were never published in any reachable source. Salas 1996 (after Aguilera 1982/83): free over the last three syllables, non-contrastive (esdrújula/grave/aguda all keep the same meaning). Hence free, non-contrastive variation in placement within a right-edge window, with a penultimate tendency at most.
4581.srule: Exists, placement not given: Aguilera 1978: 58 occasionally writes a grave accent in the lexicon 'cuando se marca un acento de menor intensidad' (e.g. jeksór-pàs, same page) but states no rule for it; Aguilera 2012 (apud Mineduc 2023: 99): 'Solo se marca el acento primario'. 4582.dq: In Kemant, all words have stress in isolation, but some may lose it in context.
4582.prule: No placement rule stated by any reachable source. Kemant is affirmed as a stress language (not tone): every word carries stress in isolation, some words lose it in context; plural suffixes attract stress. Appleyard (1991) hedges that the system 'may have moved, or be moving towards a predictable, syllable-counting stress-based system' but names no syllable. The two Addis Ababa theses (Tsige 2009, Zelealem 2000) treat only gemination and vowel length under 'Suprasegmentals' and say nothing about stress.

4584.tone: The sketch describes an accent system, not tone; it makes no statement that Quapaw lacks tone. Rankin: 'Accent is distinctive in Quapaw'; Proto-Siouan reconstructed with pitch accent ('high pitch on the second (proto) syllable counting from the left', fn. 11 p. 494 on mora-counting Crow/Hidatsa/Mandan/Winnebago); Koontz considering a pitch-accent analysis for Omaha 'and the same may be possible for Quapaw'. Rankin nonetheless writes accent 'as simple stress', so the phonetic nature (stress vs pitch) is left open; the placement rule is what is coded here.

4584.exc_quote: In general, Quapaw preserves the second syllable (iambic) accent rule, but because of the syncope of initial syllable vowels in certain forms throughout Mississippi Valley Siouan, there are numerous exceptions to the rule. Generally one can expect to find initial syllable accent in stative verb stems, body part terms, and in words beginning with a tense stop or any consonant cluster, as such forms quite generally had an initial syllable vowel that has been lost. Accent in verbs is especially fluid, often moving leftward as prefixes are added. (sec. 5.5, p. 466)
